topics.name: Field due to a current: wire, loop and solenoid

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: the compass in a strong field
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The needle of a compass, kept in an external magnetic field, always aligns itself in the North-South direction of the Earth.
Reason (R): The behaviour of the needle of the compass is similar to the behaviour of a freely suspended bar magnet.
opts: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
steps: ① A compass needle is a tiny bar magnet ✓ R true
② It lines up with whatever magnetic field acts on it
③ Only Earth's field ⟹ it points North-South
④ Strong external field ⟹ it follows THAT field ✗ A false
∴ A false, R true → (d)
questions.ans: Option (d) A is false, but R is true
questions.remember: A compass needle is a small bar magnet: it aligns along the NET magnetic field at that point. Only when Earth's field is the only one does it point North-South.
questions.trap: Choosing (a): the word 'always' makes A false. Near a strong magnet the needle points along the magnet's field.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 12 · Section 12.1 Magnetic field and field lines
questions.tryit: Which way does a compass needle point just to the right of a bar magnet's N pole?
questions.tryans: Away from the magnet: its N end points to the right, along the field

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: reverse both current and field
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Direction of force exerted on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field remains same if the directions of both magnetic field and current flowing through the conductor are reversed.
Reason (R): The direction of force exerted on a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field can be determined by using magnetic compass.
opts: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
steps: ① Force on the conductor: Fleming's left-hand rule
② Reverse the current ⟹ force reverses
③ Reverse the field too ⟹ it reverses again: back to the start ✓ A true
④ The force direction comes from Fleming's rule, not a compass ✗ R false
∴ A true, R false → (c)
questions.ans: Option (c) A is true, but R is false
questions.remember: Force on a current-carrying conductor ⟂ to a field: Fleming's LEFT-hand rule. Forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force.
questions.trap: Thinking a compass gives the force direction. A compass shows the field, not the force on a conductor.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 12 · Section 12.4 Force on a current-carrying conductor
questions.tryit: What happens to the force if only the magnetic field is reversed?

questions.title: Make an electromagnet stronger
questions.text: How is an electromagnet made? Write any two ways by which the strength of an electromagnet can be increased.
steps: ① Wind insulated copper wire into a solenoid
② Put a soft iron core inside it
③ Pass current: the core becomes a strong magnet
④ Stronger: increase the number of turns
⑤ Stronger: increase the current
∴ Solenoid + soft iron core · more turns · more current
questions.ans: Wind insulated copper wire into a coil (solenoid) round a soft iron core and pass current through it. Strength increases with (i) more turns in the coil and (ii) a larger current (also: a soft iron core).
questions.remember: Electromagnet = solenoid + soft iron core. Strength ↑ with number of turns, current, and the core. It is a magnet only while current flows.
questions.trap: Using a steel core: steel keeps its magnetism, giving a permanent magnet, not an electromagnet.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 12 · Section 12.3.3 Field due to a current in a solenoid
questions.tryit: Why is soft iron used, not steel?
questions.tryans: Soft iron loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops

questions.title: The solenoid's field lines
questions.text:
(a) What is a solenoid? Draw the magnetic field pattern due to a current-carrying solenoid (inside and outside).
(b) Name any two factors on which the magnitude of the magnetic field due to a current-carrying solenoid depends.
steps: ① Solenoid: a coil of many circular turns of insulated wire, wrapped like a cylinder
② Inside: parallel straight lines ⟹ the field is uniform
③ Outside: lines like a bar magnet, N at one end, S at the other
④ Factor 1: number of turns
⑤ Factor 2: strength of the current
∴ Uniform field inside · depends on turns and current
questions.ans: (a) A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder. Inside, the field lines are parallel straight lines (uniform field); outside, the pattern is like a bar magnet's. (b) The number of turns and the current through it (also the core material).
questions.remember: Solenoid field = bar magnet field outside, UNIFORM inside (parallel, equally spaced lines). One end acts as N, the other as S.
questions.trap: Drawing curved or crossing lines inside. Inside a solenoid they are straight, parallel and equally spaced.
questions.tryit: Where is the field of a solenoid strongest: inside or just outside?

questions.title: A rod in a horseshoe magnet
questions.text:
A metallic conductor is suspended perpendicular to the magnetic field of a horseshoe magnet. The conductor gets displaced towards the left when a current is passed through it. What will be the effect on the displacement of the conductor if the:
(I) current through the conductor is increased?
(II) horseshoe magnet is replaced by another stronger horseshoe magnet?
(III) direction of current through the conductor is reversed?
steps: ① Force ⟂ to both current and field: Fleming's left-hand rule
② Size of force grows with current and field strength
③ (I) More current ⟹ more force ⟹ displaced MORE to the left
④ (II) Stronger magnet ⟹ more force ⟹ displaced MORE to the left
⑤ (III) Current reversed ⟹ force reversed ⟹ displaced to the RIGHT
∴ More left · more left · right
questions.ans: (I) It is displaced more towards the left (larger force) · (II) It is displaced more towards the left (stronger field, larger force) · (III) It is displaced towards the right (force reverses)
questions.remember: Force on the conductor increases with current and with field strength; its direction reverses if EITHER the current OR the field is reversed (Fleming's left-hand rule).
questions.trap: (I) and (II): saying the direction changes. Only the SIZE of the displacement changes; it still goes left.
questions.tryit: What if the current and the magnet's poles are both reversed?
questions.tryans: It is displaced to the left again

questions.title: Field lines and the right-hand thumb rule
questions.text:
(i) Draw a diagram showing the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet. Write any two characteristics of magnetic field lines.
(ii) Write the statement of the Right-hand thumb rule.
(iii) The concentric circles representing the magnetic field around a current-carrying straight wire become larger and larger as we move away from the wire. How does the magnetic field change on these concentric circles?
steps: ① Lines leave N, enter S outside the magnet; inside, S to N: closed curves
② No two field lines ever cross
③ Closer lines ⟹ stronger field (crowded near the poles)
④ Thumb rule: hold the wire in the right hand, thumb along the current
⑤ The curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field
⑥ Farther from the wire ⟹ the field gets weaker
∴ Closed, never cross · thumb = I, fingers = B · weaker outward
questions.ans: (i) Field lines emerge from N and enter S outside the magnet (S to N inside), forming closed curves; no two lines cross; they are crowded where the field is strong. (ii) Hold the current-carrying wire in the right hand with the thumb along the current: the curled fingers show the direction of the field. (iii) The field decreases as the distance from the wire increases.
questions.remember: Field lines: closed curves, N to S outside, never cross, crowded = strong. Straight wire: concentric circles, B ∝ I and B ∝ 1/distance.
questions.trap: Saying field lines can cross. If they crossed, a compass at that point would point two ways at once.
questions.tryit: Why do two field lines never cross?
questions.tryans: At the crossing point the compass needle would point in two directions at once, which is impossible

questions.title: The three wires: live, neutral, earth
questions.text:
A person was repairing an electric heater. He observed that there were three different connecting wires of three different colours in the cable attached to the heater.
(i) What are these three different wires called? Name them colourwise.
(ii) What is the value of the standard potential difference at which electricity is supplied in Indian homes for lighting?
(iii) What is the role of (I) earthing and (II) fuse in domestic electric circuits?
steps: ① Live wire (positive): red insulation
② Neutral wire (negative): black insulation
③ Earth wire: green insulation
④ Supply in Indian homes: 220 V (AC, 50 Hz)
⑤ Earthing: a low-resistance path for leaking current ⟹ no severe shock
⑥ Fuse: melts if the current is too high (overloading, short circuit)
∴ Red · black · green · 220 V · earth = safety from shock · fuse = safety from excess current
questions.ans: (i) Live wire (red), neutral wire (black), earth wire (green) · (ii) 220 V (AC, 50 Hz) · (iii) Earthing gives a low-resistance path for any current leaking to the metal body, keeping its potential at earth's and preventing a severe shock; the fuse melts and breaks the circuit when the current becomes too high (overloading or short-circuiting), protecting the circuit and appliances.
questions.remember: Live = red, neutral = black, earth = green. Indian supply: 220 V AC, 50 Hz. Earthing protects PEOPLE from shocks; the fuse protects the CIRCUIT from excess current.
questions.trap: Mixing up the roles: the fuse does not stop shocks from a leaky metal body; earthing does.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 12 · Section 12.5 Domestic electric circuits
questions.tryit: Why do metal-bodied appliances use a three-pin plug?
questions.tryans: The third pin connects the metal body to earth, so a leakage current goes to earth instead of through the user
